papers.what_it_is: An independent-researcher simulation study of quantum fidelity and projected kernels against tuned classical kernels, with a 324-cell factorial design, four real datasets, a shots-versus-noise ablation and a hardware circuit-count cost model.

assertions.value: The authors state that Tier A is a full factorial over dimensionality 2, 4, 6 and 8 (equal to the qubit count), training size 50, 100 and 200, Bayes error 0.01, 0.10 and 0.25, and three data structures, with 3 independent data seeds per cell, and that it comprises 324 cells.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A, p.3; Abstract, p.1
quotes: Full factorial over dimensionality d ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8} (= qubit count), training size n ∈ {50, 100, 200}, Bayes error ∈ {0.01, 0.10, 0.25}, and three data structures, with 3 independent data seeds per cell
factorial design of 324 cells
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental design in Section IV A and the abstract.
assertions.reader_inference: Table II lists 108 cells per structure, so 324 counts the 108 factor combinations times 3 seeds; the introduction says "324 cells with three data seeds each", which reads as 324 before seeds.

assertions.value: The authors state that three controls were imposed: the bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical gamma, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations.
quotes: The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical γ, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own protocol controls in the abstract and Section IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that Tier B repeats the protocol on four standard datasets as an external-validity check, Tier C separates finite sampling from gate and readout noise, and Tier D measures cost in hardware circuit evaluations instead of simulator wall-clock.
quotes: B repeats the protocol on four standard datasets as an external-validity check. Tier C separates finite sampling from gate and readout noise
Tier D measures cost in hardware circuit evaluations instead of simulator wall-clock.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I states the four-tier design.

assertions.value: The authors state that an ad-hoc dataset generated by the feature map itself serves as a positive control: a correct implementation must win there, so a null result elsewhere can be attributed to the method and not to a bug.
quotes: an ad-hoc dataset generated by the feature map itself serves as a positive control: a correct implementation must win there
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I and IV A define the positive control as part of the protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that hypotheses and analysis choices were committed before any results existed, and that they were registered before any experiment was run.
assertions.anchor: Section I, p.2; Section IX, p.9
quotes: Hypotheses and analysis choices were committed before any results existed.
registered before any experiment was run
assertions.reader_inference: The paper offers no registry link or timestamp for the pre-registration; the statement is an author assertion.

assertions.value: The authors state that classes in the adhoc data are the most positive and most negative half of a fixed pool, not samples passing a fixed threshold, because the observable concentrates with qubit count: measured mean |<O>| falls from 0.399 at d = 2 to 0.049 at d = 8, so a fixed threshold accepted 58.6% of draws at d = 2 and 0.0% at d = 8.
quotes: Classes in adhoc are the most positive and most negative n/2 of a fixed pool, not samples passing a fixed |⟨O⟩| > gap threshold.
Measured mean |⟨O⟩| falls from 0.399 at d = 2 to 0.049 at d = 8, so a fixed threshold accepted 58.6% of draws at d = 2 and 0.0% at d = 8

assertions.value: The authors state that Bayes error is set exactly, by flipping labels of a deterministically separable labelling with the target probability, which makes separability a numeric covariate.
quotes: Bayes error is set exactly, by flipping labels of a deterministically separable labelling with the target probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV A states how the generator sets Bayes error.

assertions.value: The authors state that Tier B uses Iris (binarised), Wine (binarised), Breast Cancer Wisconsin and Ionosphere, the latter two subsampled to n=300, with features reduced by PCA to the qubit count inside each training fold.
quotes: Iris (binarised), Wine (binarised), Breast Cancer Wisconsin and Ionosphere, the latter two subsampled to n=300.
Features are reduced by PCA to the qubit count inside each training fold.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV A states the Tier B datasets and preprocessing.

assertions.value: The authors state that Tier C is a 2x4 grid of exact or 1024 shots crossed with noiseless, depolarising 0.001, depolarising 0.01 and readout 0.02, run on one Tier A cell.
quotes: A 2×4 grid of {exact, 1024 shots} × {noiseless, depolarising 0.001, depolarising 0.01, readout 0.02} on one Tier A cell
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV A states the Tier C design.

assertions.value: The authors describe the feature map without entangling terms (z) as a deliberate negative control that is classically simulable, so that if it matches the IQP-style map, entanglement is contributing nothing measurable.
quotes: The latter is a deliberate negative control. It is classically simulable, so if it matches iqp, entanglement is contributing nothing
measurable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV B defines the negative control.

assertions.value: The authors state that inputs are scaled by the bandwidth c before encoding, that c is tuned in the inner loop on the same footing as the classical gamma, and that leaving it fixed while grid-searching the RBF is the single most common way to rig this comparison.
quotes: c is tuned in the inner loop on the same footing as the classical γ; leaving it fixed while grid-searching the RBF is the single most common way to rig this comparison.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV B states the protocol; the "most common way to rig" part is the authors' characterisation of the literature.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim that this is the most common way to rig comparisons is not supported by a survey in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the bandwidth response is sharp and non-monotone: on the positive control, cross-validated accuracy runs 0.767, 1.000 and 0.567 at c = 0.81, 1.00 and 1.52.
quotes: cross-validated accuracy runs 0.767 / 1.000 / 0.567 at c = 0.81 / 1.00 / 1.52.

assertions.value: The authors report that an eight-point logarithmic grid straddled the optimum and scored the positive control at 0.742, which they would otherwise have reported as a weak quantum kernel.
quotes: an eight-point logarithmic grid straddled the optimum and scored the control at 0.742

assertions.value: The authors state that angle encoding is periodic and not shift-invariant, so standardisation alone wraps the encoding, and the pipeline ends in a MinMax map to [0, π].
quotes: Angle encoding is periodic and not shift-invariant, so standardisation alone both wraps the encoding and
the pipeline ends in a MinMax map to [0, π].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV B states the preprocessing used.

assertions.value: The authors report the hyperparameter grid sizes (Table I): quantum 91 (13 bandwidths x 7 C), SVM-RBF 77 (11 gamma x 7 C), SVM-poly 28, SVM-linear 7 and HistGradientBoosting 6, and state each baseline receives a comparable tuning budget.
assertions.anchor: Section IV C, Table I, p.4
quotes: quantum (13 bandwidths × 7 C) 91
SVM-RBF (11 γ × 7 C) 77
SVM-poly 28 SVM-linear 7 HistGradientBoosting 6
assertions.certainty_reason: Table I states the grid sizes used.
assertions.reader_inference: The grids differ in size (91 for the quantum kernel, 7 for SVM-linear, 6 for gradient boosting), so "comparable" holds for the RBF and quantum arms more than for the others.

assertions.value: The authors state the protocol is nested cross-validation with 5 stratified outer folds (Tier B repeated 3 times) and 3 stratified inner folds for all hyperparameter selection, quantum and classical alike.
quotes: Nested cross-validation: 5 stratified outer folds (Tier B: repeated 3×), 3 stratified inner folds for all hyperparameter selection, quantum and classical alike.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV D states the evaluation protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that scaler and PCA are fitted on the training fold only, that scaling changes the encoded angles so the quantum kernel is recomputed inside each fold, and that a kernel matrix computed once over the full dataset leaks test statistics into training.
quotes: Scaler and PCA are fitted on the training fold only.
a kernel matrix computed once over the full dataset leaks test statistics into training.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states a shuffled-label test guards this property but does not report a comparison of leaked and unleaked kernels.

assertions.value: The authors state that shot-based kernels can leave the PSD cone and are projected back by clipping negative eigenvalues below a tolerance, with the repair magnitude logged, and report that exact statevector kernels produce tiny negative eigenvalues on 12% of runs.
quotes: Shot-based kernels can leave the PSD cone; the matrix is projected back by clipping
exact statevector kernels produce negative eigenvalues of order 10−13 on 12% of runs
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV D states the repair procedure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the same matrix equals the squared magnitude of S S-dagger over the n encoded statevectors, so it costs O(n) circuits and one matrix product, roughly 1000x faster in simulation, used for exact runs while the O(n2) hardware figure is always reported.
quotes: so it costs O(n) circuits and one matrix product, roughly 1000× faster in simulation and identical to 10−9 in our tests.
We use that shortcut for exact runs but always report the O(n2) hardware figure
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV E states how exact runs and the cost figure are computed.

assertions.value: The authors state that on hardware a fidelity kernel costs n(n - 1)/2 circuits.
quotes: On hardware a fidelity kernel costs n(n − 1)/2 circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV E states the circuit count that the paper uses for its cost model.

assertions.value: The authors report that across 324 cells the tuned quantum kernel beats the best classical baseline in 30.2% of cells, with median accuracy delta +0.0000 and mean +0.0100.
quotes: Across 324 cells, the tuned quantum kernel beats the best classical baseline in 30.2% of cells, with median accuracy delta +0.0000 and mean +0.0100.

assertions.value: The authors report (Table II) that on the adhoc structure the per-cell accuracy delta (tuned quantum minus best classical) has mean +0.058, median +0.03 and a win rate of 65.7% over 108 cells.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, p.4; Table II, p.5
quotes: structure mean ∆ median ∆ win rate cells adhoc linear xor +0.058 +0.03 -0.002 0.00 -0.026 -0.02 65.7% 108 3.7% 108 21.3% 108
It sits almost entirely in the positive control (Table II).

quotes: structure mean ∆ median ∆ win rate cells adhoc linear xor +0.058 +0.03 -0.002 0.00 -0.026 -0.02 65.7% 108 3.7% 108 21.3% 108

quotes: structure mean ∆ median ∆ win rate cells adhoc linear xor +0.058 +0.03 -0.002 0.00 -0.026 -0.02 65.7% 108 3.7% 108 21.3% 108

assertions.value: The authors report (Table III) that in the regression of the per-cell delta on the design factors, the coefficient on dimensionality d (qubits) is -0.0045 with standard error 0.0018, t = -2.57 and p = .011.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, Table III, p.5

assertions.value: The authors report (Table III) that in the same regression the coefficient on log n is +0.0152 (standard error 0.0069, t = 2.19, p = .029) and the coefficient on Bayes error is -0.1048 (standard error 0.0397, t = -2.64, p = .009).
assertions.anchor: Section V A, Table III, p.5

assertions.value: The authors report (Table III) that the structure[linear] coefficient is -0.0601 (t = -6.25) and the structure[xor] coefficient is -0.0836 (t = -8.69), both p < .001, and that the regression has R2 = 0.237 over 324 cells.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, Table III, p.5
quotes: design factors (R2 = 0.237, 324 cells)
assertions.reader_inference: R2 = 0.237 means the design factors explain under a quarter of the variance in the per-cell delta.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum advantage shrinks with dimensionality, grows with training size, shrinks as classes overlap, and is dominated by whether the data was generated by a quantum feature map at all.
quotes: the quantum advantage shrinks with dimensionality, grows with training size, shrinks as classes overlap, and is dominated by whether the data was generated by a quantum feature map at all.

assertions.value: The authors report that the xor delta degrades monotonically with d (-0.016, -0.027, -0.029, -0.032 at d = 2, 4, 6, 8), while adhoc peaks at d = 4 (+0.153) and decays to +0.006 by d = 8.
quotes: The xor column degrades monotonically with d (-0.016, -0.027, -0.029, -0.032 at d = 2, 4, 6, 8), while adhoc peaks at d = 4 (+0.153) and decays to +0.006 by d = 8.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 1: the tuned-quantum minus best-classical accuracy delta is negative in every cell of the dimensionality (about 2 to about 8 qubits) by training-size (about 50 to about 200) grid, from about -0.1 at about 2 qubits and about 200 training samples to about -0.2 or lower at about 4 to about 8 qubits and about 50 training samples, and the delta is closer to zero at larger training size.
quotes: FIG. 1. Accuracy of the tuned quantum kernel minus the best classical baseline, over dimensionality and training size.
assertions.reader_inference: Every cell in the heat map is blue (negative), yet the text reports a mean delta of +0.0100 over all 324 cells and Table II gives positive adhoc deltas. The caption does not say how cells are aggregated, so the figure and the text may use different aggregations (for example a worst case); the paper does not explain it.

assertions.value: The authors report that across tuned Tier A folds the selected bandwidth is bimodal: 1,900 folds select the grid floor c = 0.01 and 733 select c = 1.0, with the remainder spread across the decade grid.
quotes: across tuned Tier A folds it is bimodal, 1,900 folds
selecting the grid floor c = 0.01 and 733 selecting c = 1.0, with the remainder spread across the decade grid.

assertions.value: The authors report (Table IV) that on Tier A synthetic data the tuned-bandwidth accuracy is 0.726 against 0.606 for the untuned (c = 1) map, a gap of +0.120.
assertions.anchor: Section V B, Table IV, p.5
quotes: tuned bandwidth 0.726 untuned (c = 1) 0.606 gap +0.120 0.956 0.617 +0.339

assertions.value: The authors report (Table IV) that on Tier B real data the tuned-bandwidth accuracy is 0.956 against 0.617 for the untuned (c = 1) map, a gap of +0.339, on identical circuits and identical data.
assertions.anchor: Section V B, Table IV, p.5; Section I, p.2
quotes: tuned bandwidth 0.726 untuned (c = 1) 0.606 gap +0.120 0.956 0.617 +0.339
An untuned quantum kernel scores 0.617 on real data and a tuned one 0.956, on identical circuits and identical data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the bandwidth effect (0.120 accuracy on synthetic data, 0.339 on real data) is larger than any quantum-versus-classical difference they observe and larger than the margins reported in the studies that disagree with each other.
quotes: Tuning the feature map’s bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real datasets.
Both figures are larger than any quantum-versus-classical difference we observe, and larger than the margins reported
in the studies that disagree with each other.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison to published margins is the authors' statement; the paper does not tabulate those published margins.

assertions.value: The authors claim that a published comparison that tunes the classical gamma but fixes the quantum bandwidth is measuring its own protocol, not the kernels, and that protocol variance is sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.
assertions.anchor: Section V B, p.5; Abstract, p.1
quotes: A published comparison that tunes the classical γ but fixes the quantum bandwidth is measuring its own protocol, not the kernels.
Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field’s contradictory conclusions.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not re-run any published comparison; the sufficiency claim rests on its own effect sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that their result does not prove that any specific published result is an artifact, but removes the need to invoke properties of quantum kernels to explain why the literature disagrees with itself.
quotes: This does not prove that any
specific published result is an artifact, but it removes the need to invoke properties of quantum kernels to explain why the literature disagrees with itself.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their inference in the Discussion.

assertions.value: The authors report that paired Nadeau-Bengio corrected t-tests against a tuned RBF give no significant difference on any Tier B dataset, for either kernel family, before or after Holm-Bonferroni correction.
quotes: Paired Nadeau–Bengio corrected t-tests against a tuned RBF give no significant difference on any
dataset, for either kernel family, before or after Holm–Bonferroni correction.

papers.what_it_is: A random-matrix-theory analysis of quantum linear regression (quantum extreme learning machines and fidelity kernels) with finite measurement shots, deriving a triple-descent error profile with a classical peak at informational completeness and a quantum peak at the interpolation threshold, with ridge regularization, theorems and proofs in a long supplement.

assertions.value: The authors state that as the number of measurement outcomes grows, the prediction error of quantum linear regression displays a triple-descent profile with two peaks of fundamentally different origins.
quotes: As the number of measurement outcomes grows, the prediction error displays a triple-descent profile, with two peaks of fundamentally different origins.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement is the abstract summary of the analytical results (Theorems 2 to 4) and the simulations.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first, classical, peak occurs when the measurement first becomes informationally complete, is a direct analogue of double descent in classical linear regression and is caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement itself; it affects predictions only through their variance and is thus suppressed by increasing the number of shots at inference.
quotes: The first, classical, peak occurs when the measurement first becomes informationally complete, is a direct
analogue of double descent in classical linear regression, and is caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement itself.
This peak affects predictions only through their variance, and is thus suppressed by increasing the number of shots at inference.

assertions.value: The authors state that the second, quantum, peak occurs beyond informational completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states: shot noise populates unphysical outcome combinations and the regression fits these pure-noise features with large weights, corrupting the learned model itself; more training or test shots cannot remove it, and it disappears only in the ideal limit of exact training features.
quotes: The second, quantum, peak occurs beyond

informational completeness when the number of outcomes matches the number of training states: shot noise populates unphysical outcome combinations and the regression fits these pure-noise features with large weights, corrupting the learned model itself.
More training or test shots cannot remove this
quantum peak, which disappears only in the ideal limit of exact training features.

assertions.value: The authors state that using random-matrix theory they derive the shape of both peaks analytically, also accounting for ridge regularization, and that treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones.
quotes: Using random-matrix theory, we derive the shape of both peaks analytically, accounting also for ridge regularization.
Our results show that treating quantum features as exactly known overestimates classical
instabilities while missing genuinely quantum ones.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum linear regression (QLR) models, a class that includes quantum extreme learning machines, quantum reservoir computing and quantum fidelity kernels, use a quantum device to produce features as expectation values of fixed measurement operators and a prediction that is a linear combination of these features with coefficients fitted classically by standard regression.
quotes: Quantum linear regression — We study these effects in quantum linear regression (QLR) models [5], a class of QML protocols that includes quantum extreme learning machines [6–11],
quantum reservoir computing [12–14], and quantum fidelity kernels [3, 4, 15, 16].

In QLR, a quantum device produces the features as expectation values of fixed measurement operators, and the prediction is a linear combination of these features whose coefficients are fitted classically by standard
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I defines the model class studied.

assertions.value: The authors state that sampling noise can produce effects that do not vanish with more shots and that reducing it can even worsen performance in some cases, citing their companion paper [5] that showed standard training methods can end up fitting the sampling noise itself, a form of quantum overfitting that worsens as the training statistics increase.
quotes: this picture is incomplete: sampling noise can produce effects that do not vanish with more shots, and reducing it can even worsen performance in some cases.
In a companion paper [5], for example, we showed that standard training methods can
end up fitting the sampling noise itself, a form of quantum overfitting that worsens as the training statistics increase.

assertions.value: The authors state that in ridgeless and random-feature regression double descent arises because the feature matrix is square when the number of features matches the number of training examples, and random matrix theory shows square random matrices typically have singular values close to zero.
quotes: The peak arises because the feature matrix is square at that point, and random matrix theory shows that square random matrices typically have singular values close to zero

assertions.value: The authors state that sampling noise adds a second peak producing a triple descent as the number of measurement outcomes is varied, that this new peak has an intrinsically stochastic origin so that more training statistics do not suppress it (in the test variance its height grows and then saturates to a value depending on the dimension), and that it disappears only in the theoretical limit of exactly known training features.
quotes: Here, we show that sampling noise adds a second peak to this picture, producing a triple descent as the number of measurement outcomes is varied.
this new peak has an

intrinsically stochastic origin: more training statistics do not suppress it — in the test variance, its height actually grows and then saturates to a value depending on the dimension — and it disappears only in the theoretical limit of exactly known training features.

assertions.value: The authors state that they focus on the simplest quantum features, the outcome probabilities of a fixed measurement after a fixed quantum evolution, and that the mechanisms they identify rely only on two properties shared by all QLR models: the exact features depend linearly on the input state and are estimated from finite samples.
quotes: We focus our analysis on the simplest type of quantum
features: the outcome probabilities of a fixed measurement performed after a fixed quantum evolution.
the mechanisms we identify rely only on
two properties shared by all QLR models: the exact features depend linearly on the input state, and they are
estimated from finite samples.

assertions.value: The authors define a peak as classical if it is caused by ill-conditioning of the exact feature matrix, typically inherited from the measurement itself, and quantum if it is caused by nearly singular directions that sampling fluctuations create; in both cases the peak appears because a random matrix close to square is likely to be nearly singular, as described by the Marchenko-Pastur law.
quotes: We call a peak classical if it is caused by ill-conditioning of the exact feature matrix, typically inherited from the measurement itself, and
quantum if it is caused by nearly singular

directions that sampling fluctuations create. In both cases, the peak appears because a random matrix that is close to square is likely to be nearly singular, as described by the Marchenko–Pastur law.

exhibits a classical peak at the threshold for informational completeness, nout = d2, caused by ill-conditioning of the measurement frame.

Because this peak stems from large exact
regression coefficients, its effect on predictions is confined to their variance, and more shots at inference suppress it.

assertions.value: The authors state that for n_out > d^2 a further classical peak can occur at n_tr = d^2 when the training labels are noisy, even with exact measurement probabilities, because near this threshold the training states become nearly linearly dependent while the corresponding combinations of noisy labels do not vanish; the peak persists even for N = M = infinity and does not occur in the absence of label noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that at the interpolation threshold n_out = n_tr the classification depends on informational completeness: for n_tr < d^2 the exact training-feature matrix can itself become poorly conditioned and the peak is classical, while for n_tr > d^2 the peak is quantum, because exact probabilities span at most d^2 dimensions but training-shot fluctuations populate the remaining directions; consequently adding outcomes beyond informational completeness can worsen predictions even as the measurement frame becomes better conditioned.

are rounded and their heights fluctuate across measurements and training records.

papers.what_it_is: A simulator study comparing parameterized quantum circuits (simple and data re-uploading) with fully connected neural networks on three test regression functions and on predicting GPU temperatures in DGX A100 servers from 16 telemetry inputs.

assertions.value: The authors state that they trained a quantum circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPUs of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters.
quotes: We trained a quantum
circuit to predict the temperature of each of the eight GPU of each cluster node based on 16 physical parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the task the paper addresses.

assertions.value: The authors claim that quantum machine learning performs on the GPU-temperature task just as well as classical machine learning, and that, using model problems, quantum machine learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.
quotes: We demonstrated that quantum machine learning performs on this task just as well as classical machine learning.
using model problems, we demonstrated that quantum machine
learning can potentially outperform classical machine learning.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported MAD values (1.41 for the best quantum circuit against 1.35 and 1.46 for the two neural networks) come from single runs without repeated trials or error bars, so "just as well" is not tested statistically.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum computer simulator was used for modeling the quantum circuit and that calculations are carried out without taking noise into account.
quotes: We used simulator of quantum
computer for modeling quantum circuit. Calculations are carried out without taking into account the noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states that all computations are noiseless simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that all computations were performed on a quantum device simulator, and that the results show this approach can be implemented on a real quantum computer.
quotes: All computations were performed on a quantum device simulator.
a real quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 8 states that all computations were run on a simulator.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement that the approach can be implemented on a real quantum computer is not tested in the paper; no hardware run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that they did not inject quantum noise into the simulation of the test-function experiments (fidelity = 1).
quotes: We didn’t injected the quantum noise (Figure 2) till the simulation (fidelity = 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states the simulation setting.

assertions.value: The authors state that the node servers are NVIDIA DGX A100 servers, each with 8 NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs, and that telemetry data is collected via the BMC port.
quotes: The node servers are the DGX A100 servers from NVidia, which includes:
8x NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs with 640 GB Total GPU Memory
Telemetry data is collected via the BMC port.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the data source.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of analyzed parameter values exceeded 10M, collected over a period of over six months, as a multivariate time series supplemented by server downtime information.
quotes: The number of analyzed parameter values exceeded 10M, collected over a period
of over six months.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the dataset size and collection period.

assertions.value: The authors state that the telemetry dataset used in the Results contains 270,000 parameter measurements, that a random sample of 10% of the original dataset was used for training, and that the data was split into train (70%), validation (15%) and test (15%).
quotes: The telemetry dataset contains 270,000
parameter measurements.
For training, we used a random sample of 10% of the original dataset.
train (70%), validation (15%), and test data (15%)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6 states the data split.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 3 gives more than 10M values for the full data and Section 6 gives 270,000 measurements; the paper does not reconcile the two figures or say how many records the 10% sample holds.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the server operating temperature rises to a threshold of 80 degrees Celsius the server automation increases the fan rotation speed, and when the threshold is exceeded it reduces power consumption and performance, with exact algorithms unknown and no notification to administrators.
quotes: when the server’s operating temperature rises to a threshold of 80 degrees Celsius, the server’s automation increases the fan rotation
The exact algorithms of the server’s automation are unknown
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 describes the system being modelled.

assertions.value: The authors state that a correlation analysis showed three parameters (GPU utilization, GPU temperature and GPU power consumption) provide an effective leading indicator for predicting the increased risk of server failure due to thermal issues.

temperature, and GPU Power consumption) provide an effective leading indicator for
assertions.reader_inference: The correlation analysis itself is not shown in the paper.

assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the problem formulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that their circuit design is based on the architecture of reference [24] with three circuit types (a simple quantum circuit, a quantum kernel and a re-uploading circuit), consisting of an input layer of Rx rotations, N_L identical ansatz layers of three-angle rotations with N CNOT entanglement gates, and a measurement layer giving the average Z value of each qubit.
quotes: We based our design on the
quantum circuit architecture from [24], which considers three types of quantum circuits for QML: a simple quantum circuit, a quantum kernel, and a reuploading circuit.
The layers contains N control NOT (CNOT) entanglement gates
The output of the measurement layer is the average
value of each qubit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 describes the architecture used.

assertions.value: The authors define re-uploading as including, before each ansatz layer, one additional rotator Rx with a rotation angle equal to the angle on the zero qubit of the input layer and acting on the first qubit, and call a scheme without these rotators a simple quantum circuit.
quotes: Additionally, before each ansatz layer, one additional rotator Rx(θ1in) can be included with a rotation angle equal to the rotation angle on the zero qubit of the input layer and acting on the first qubit. This scheme is called re-uploading.
A scheme without additional rotators
in the ansatz will be called a simple quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 defines the two circuit variants compared.

assertions.value: The authors state that a single linear neural-network layer is placed before the input layer and another after the output layer, because input gate arguments take values between 0 and 2π and averaged Z measurements lie between 0 and 1, while function arguments and values can have a larger range.

the average measurement values in the output layer can take values between 0 and 1.
we’ll place a single linear neural network layer before the input layer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states the design of the input and output scaling.

quotes: The total number of trainable parameters is:
Npq = (3NL + NI + NO) N + NI + NO = O (N NL) .

neurons and layers so that the values of Npq and Npc are comparable

papers.what_it_is: A theory-plus-experiment paper giving three pre-training rules for choosing a variational quantum circuit (a product-ansatz Fourier rank test, a QFIM-rank depth law, and a Pauli-Z product readout), tested on the Madelon dataset by ablation of a 239-parameter block classifier.

assertions.value: The authors state that they give three rules that fix the choices of ansatz and depth from the data and the gate set alone, before any training.
quotes: We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training.
assertions.reader_inference: The three rules are a product-ansatz test (Section 2), a depth rule (Section 3) and a readout rule (Section 4); only the second and third are used in the experiment together with the block size and block count fixed by other considerations.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the Madelon dataset the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3, a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search.

depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a
grid search.
assertions.reader_inference: The block count 7 is set by the 20 retained features and the block size 3 by a trainability threshold the authors adopt (Section 6.1). The paper reports no classical baseline on the same split other than the failure of linear models (61.5%).

assertions.value: The authors state that ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

papers.what_it_is: A quantum learning-theory paper proving a no-go theorem that a resource-constrained verifier gains no query-complexity advantage from classical interaction with an untrusted resource-unconstrained prover for many testing and learning problems, and constructing interactive proofs with quantum communication that let single-copy quantum verifiers beat even coherent multi-copy lower bounds for purity testing, tomography and stabilizer learning.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a wide variety of scenarios they prove that a resource-constrained learner cannot gain any advantage through classical interaction with an untrusted prover, and that for the vast majority of testing and learning problems in which quantum memory is a meaningful resource, a memory-constrained quantum algorithm cannot overcome its limitations via classical communication with a memory-unconstrained quantum prover.

assertions.reader_inference: The statement is the abstract summary of Theorem 1 and its corollaries; the precise conditions are in Theorem 1 (many-vs-one distinguishing, honest prover simulable on the accept instance).

assertions.value: The authors state that when quantum communication is allowed they construct a variety of interactive proof protocols, for specific learning and testing problems, which allow memory-constrained quantum verifiers to gain significant advantages through delegation to untrusted provers.

assertions.reader_inference: The concrete protocols and their proved guarantees are Theorems 2 to 5 and Section 4; this entry is the abstract-level statement.

assertions.value: The authors define a many-vs-one distinguishing problem by a triple (xA, XR, X) with X an instance set, XR a subset of X the reject set and xA in X minus XR the accept instance; the valid solution is accept for oracle access to xA, reject for any x in XR, and either answer for any other instance.
quotes: Definition 1: (Many-vs-one distinguishing problem) A many-vs-one distinguishing problem is defined by a triple (xA, XR, X ), where X is some instance set, XR ⊂ X is a reject set, and xA ∈ X \ XR is an accept instance.
(i) When given
oracle access to xA, the valid solution is “accept".
(ii) When given oracles access to x ∈ XR, the valid solution is “reject".
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 1 in Section 1.1.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 1) that if A is a class of resource-constrained algorithms such that any algorithm in A needs m oracle queries to solve the many-vs-one distinguishing task (xA, XR, X) from OV-access with probability at least 1 - delta, and (V, P) with V in A is an interactive proof system with success probability 1 - delta from (OV, OP)-access such that, for all x in X, the actions of the honest prover P with access to OP(xA), interacting with V with access to OV(x), can be simulated by an algorithm in A, then V has to make at least m oracle queries.
quotes: Theorem 1: (Limitations of interactive proofs for many-vs-one distinguishing) Let A be a class of resource-constrained algorithms such that any A ∈ A requires m oracle queries to solve the many-vs-one distinguishing task (xA, XR, X ) from OV -access, with probability ≥ 1 − δ.
If, for all x ∈ X , the actions of the honest prover P with access to OP (xA), when interacting
with V with access to OV (x), can be simulated by an algorithm in A, then V has to make at least m oracle queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 is stated with its conditions in Section 3 and proved by a simulation argument on pp.19-20.

assertions.value: The authors prove Theorem 1 by constructing a distinguisher D in A that simulates the interaction between V with access to OV(x) and P with access to OP(xA), outputting reject if the simulated V aborts or rejects and accept otherwise; by completeness D is correct for x = xA with probability at least 1 - delta, and by soundness D is correct for x in XR with probability at least 1 - delta.

If the simulated V either aborts the interaction or outputs “reject”, then D outputs “reject”. Otherwise, D outputs “accept”.
if x = xA, then by the completeness guarantee of (V , P), the simulated verifier V does not abort and correctly outputs “accept” with probability ≥ 1 − δ.
if x ∈ XR, then by the soundness guarantee of (V , P), the simulated verifier V does not abort and incorrectly outputs “accept” with probability < δ.
assertions.certainty_reason: The proof of Theorem 1 is given in full in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the no-go theorem the class A is not required to simulate the honest prover with access to any OP(x); it only needs to simulate the prover in an interaction where V has oracle access to an arbitrary x in X but P has access to OP(xA), the oracle of the accept instance.

assertions.value: The authors state an extension of the no-go theorem to computational complexity: if an interactive proof lets V in A use computational time CV, some algorithm in A can simulate the honest prover with access to the accept instance oracle in time CP, and any algorithm in A needs at least CA time, then CV + CP is at least CA, so CV is at least CA - CP.
quotes: we straightforwardly obtain a version
for computational complexities when taking the computational cost of simulating P into account.
if a lower bound of CA computational time exists for any algorithm in A, then one must have CV + CP ≥ CA so CV ≥ CA − CP .
assertions.reader_inference: The extension is stated informally ("Informally, let us assume") and not as a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a learning problem with an underlying easier-than-learning many-vs-one distinguishing task, if an interactive proof for the learning problem needs ml verifier queries, solving the distinguishing task given a valid learning solution needs ml-to-d queries, and solving the distinguishing task in isolation needs md queries, then Theorem 1 implies ml + ml-to-d is at least md, so ml is at least md - ml-to-d.
quotes: Theorem 1 then implies that    ml + ml→d ≥ md ,    (4)
and therefore that ml ≥ md −ml→d , which can be non-trivial whenever ml→d is sufficiently small.

cannot gain any advantage in query complexity by delegating a many-vs-one distinguishing task to the prover via an interactive proof.
1. Purity testing [Che+22b].
3. State certification and mixedness testing [Che+22c].
4. Unitarity testing [Che+22b; Che+23a].

assertions.value: The authors state two drawbacks of the VBQC-based approach: V needs to know the circuit implementing the measurement it would run if it could process multiple copies coherently, and all the quantum data comes from the verifier's oracle OV so OP is not used, so V can overcome single-copy lower bounds but never multi-copy lower bounds.

of VBQC protocols in our context, V needs to know the circuit (implementing the measurement) that they would run to solve the problem at hand
all the quantum data comes from the verifier’s oracle OV ; the oracle OP is not
used at all. So, this way V can overcome single-copy lower bounds through interaction with P, but it can never surpass multi-copy lower bounds.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.3.2 states the limits of the generic VBQC-based protocol.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since in the classical-verifier protocols of [RUV13; Col+24; Mah22] the verifier is entirely classical and communication is necessarily classical, Theorem 1 implies that none of these interactive verification protocols enable the verifier to achieve query complexity advantages for the learning and testing problems discussed.

assertions.value: The authors state that their framework extends the framework of interactive proofs for PAC verification of [Gol+21] and that their work initiates the study of quantum learning and testing problems in the delegated setting, so there is no prior work on concrete protocols or inherent limitations with which to directly compare their upper and lower bounds.
quotes: the framework we use here, described in Section 1.1, extends the framework of interactive proofs for PAC verification recently introduced in Ref. [Gol+21].

we stress that our work initiates the study of quantum learning and testing problems in the delegated setting, and as such there is no prior work on either concrete protocols, or inherent limitations with which to directly compare the upper and lower bounds we obtain.

assertions.value: The authors state that without computational assumptions it is currently a major open question whether classical communication suffices for the delegation of quantum computation or whether a little bit of quantumness is needed, and that their impossibility results with classical communication for delegating learning and testing on data highlight the distinctive role of data and may inspire new approaches to that question.
